paragraphs.text: The mild variant of congenital myopathy-10B (CMYO10B) is an autosomal recessive myopathy with onset in infancy or childhood of predominantly axial and proximal weakness, often beginning in the neck, together with facial weakness, joint contractures, scoliosis, and respiratory insufficiency that develops later in childhood or beyond. Muscle biopsy may show minicores, sometimes together with dystrophic or myofibrillar changes (Boyden et al., 2012; Croci et al., 2022). The disorder is milder than the severe early-onset form of MEGF10-related myopathy with areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD) (Takayama et al., 2016; Harris et al., 2018).

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) reported a nonconsanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had a myopathy that resembled multiminicore disease in some respects. Weakness began by 12 months of age, at first in the neck. It affected the whole body but was mainly axial and proximal, with facial weakness, and it stabilized in adolescence. Neck contractures were seen in infancy, and contractures of the elbows, knees, and heel cords had developed by adulthood. Serum creatine kinase measured before age 10 years was mildly elevated. All 3 patients had scoliosis from childhood that was treated with spinal fusion. From age 10 to 11 years, all 3 developed respiratory problems treated with nocturnal bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation. One patient was born with a cleft palate, a second had a midline ridge on her palate in adulthood, and all 3 had hypernasal speech. Muscle biopsies showed dystrophic features, including fatty replacement of myofibers, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers. Moth-eaten fibers and minicores were also present. Rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, central cores, nemaline rods, and ragged red fibers were absent. There was a slight predominance of type I fibers. Before genetic testing, the patients had been diagnosed with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy or spinal muscular atrophy.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) also described a female Caucasian patient (subject 105-1) of distant Portuguese ancestry who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease. She presented at several weeks of age with hypotonia, a weak neck, and a floppy head. She had a markedly high-arched palate, failure to thrive due to poor feeding, blue-tinged sclerae, and hyperflexible joints. She had frequent acute pulmonary infections in childhood but no chronic breathing problems. At age 10 years, serum CK was mildly elevated at 302 U/L, and mild scoliosis was present; it progressed to 20 degrees by age 12 years. Her weakness was mild, nonprogressive, and mainly proximal, and included facial weakness. Muscle biopsy showed minicores, which were confirmed by electron microscopy.

paragraphs.text: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man born to healthy consanguineous parents. He was born at 33 weeks' gestation and needed resuscitation for asphyxia. He had a weak suck, and elbow contractures and scoliosis were present from the first months of life. Motor development and intellect were normal. He developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia, and respiratory involvement. The case report states that he needed nocturnal noninvasive ventilation from age 16 years, whereas the discussion states that he needed respiratory support at age 6. Serum CK, brain and spine MRI, ECG, and echocardiogram were normal. Nerve conduction was normal apart from reduced compound muscle action potential amplitudes. Follow-up examination showed axial hypotonia, generalized muscle hypotrophy and weakness, preserved facial expression, cleft palate, global areflexia, and contractures of the elbows and ankles. He could walk without support but used a manual wheelchair for longer distances. He had Achilles tendon tenotomy and vertebral arthrodesis. From age 17 years, he had swallowing difficulties and recurrent pulmonary infections due to aspiration of food. A first muscle biopsy at age 5 years showed nonspecific changes: fiber size variation, internal nuclei, and fibrosis. A second biopsy showed myofibrillar alterations, including whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions, and minicores.

paragraphs.text: In the 3 affected sibs of family 1030 with a congenital myopathy with minicores, Boyden et al. (2012) identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the MEGF10 gene: c.976T-C (C326R) and c.2320T-C (C774R). The mutations were found by whole-genome sequencing of 1 affected sib, with variants filtered using linkage data. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the mutations were in trans and segregated with the disorder in all 6 family members. Neither mutation was present in dbSNP, the 1000 Genomes Project, the Exome Sequencing Project, or 56 internal genomes. The c.976T-C and c.2320T-C mutations were absent from 715 and 645 genotyped controls, respectively. Both mutations replace cysteine residues in atypical EGF-like domains that are completely conserved in 43 species. Knockdown of megf10 in zebrafish with 4 different morpholinos caused curved tails, impaired motility, unhatched eggs, reduced birefringence, and disorganized muscle tissue.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) also sequenced the MEGF10 open reading frame in 190 patients with genetically unexplained myopathies. They found a single heterozygous mutation, c.211C-T (R71W), in subject 105-1, whose clinical and histologic presentation resembled that of family 1030. agent.process_note: I read the full texts of Boyden et al. (2012) and Croci et al. (2022), and the abstracts of Takayama et al. (2016) and Harris et al. (2018), which are the only parts available. For Holterman et al. (2007), a mouse satellite-cell study, I read the abstract and introduction and used Grep to find the knockdown and Notch findings. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so the intro gives no gene MIM number; the chromosome 5 location comes from Boyden's linkage result. The abstracts do not give the nucleotide change for C810Y, and Harris's abstract does not explicitly say compound heterozygous, so I left those details out. Croci's report contradicts itself on when respiratory support began (age 16 vs age 6) and on the interval between the two biopsies; I described the respiratory discrepancy and left the biopsy interval unstated. Boyden's single heterozygous R71W patient is described, but not listed as an allelic variant, because a second mutation was not found.
